transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, honestly, what brings me in is... I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. And I mean, I've been doing carpentry since I got out of high school, almost forty years, so I know my way around a shop. I know how to work. But lately, it's like every little thing pulls me away. 

I'll be in the middle of measuring a cut, and just one saw starting up across the floor—just that noise—and I'm completely derailed. I'm wondering who's running it, if they're using the right blade, what they're working on. Or somebody walking past the office window. I'll stop what I'm doing just to see who it is and where they're going. 

Sometimes it's not even something happening around me, it's just my own head. Like, I’ll get a random thought about another job we've got lined up for next week, and suddenly I'm walking away from my workbench to go check the lumber order for that other job, completely abandoning the piece that's right in front of me. And then I'll find something else over by the desk, and I'll start doing that, and it just keeps going like a chain reaction until the whole day gets away from me. I’ll look at the clock and it’s quitting time, and I haven’t finished the one simple cabinet door I started at eight in the morning. It’s just... it’s exhausting, to be honest with you, because I'm trying so hard to just do the work, but I just get pulled off what I’m doing constantly, every single day, and I can't afford to keep losing time like this.
Are you having trouble meeting deadlines or fulfilling your responsibilities at work due to these distractions?

Oh, absolutely. It’s... it's really becoming a serious problem. I mean, it’s not just that I’m frustrated, it’s actually costing me. Just last month, I lost a commission on a custom dining table—a really beautiful cherry wood piece that I was so excited about—because I missed the deadline by three weeks. Three weeks! The client just got fed up and pulled the job. And the rework... oh, the rework. Because I get distracted halfway through measuring or cutting, I end up making mistakes that I wouldn't have made ten years ago. I cut a piece too short because I was thinking about the hardware order, and then I have to scrap it and start over. Wood isn't cheap right now, you know? It eats right into the profit margin. 

And the crew... well, I’ve been working with some of these guys for years, and I can tell they’re getting frustrated with me. They used to rely on me to handle the scheduling for the shop and to make sure the lumber orders were in on time, but now? Now they kind of step around me and just do it themselves. I heard one of the younger guys say the other day, "Don't give that to Sarah, it'll just sit on her desk until Christmas." It stings, you know? It really stings, because I know how to do this job, but I just... I can't seem to execute it anymore.

And it’s not just at the shop, either. It bleeds into everything. My husband, bless his heart, he’s had to completely take over the household stuff. The bills, the reminders, all of it. I used to handle all the paperwork, but lately, I’ll bring the mail in, set it on the kitchen counter to sort it, and then I’ll notice the dog needs water, so I go do that, and then I see a spot on the floor, so I start mopping, and the mail just sits there. Next thing I know, we’re getting a late notice on the electric bill because I misplaced the first one under a stack of magazines I was meaning to read. Or he'll tell me we need to call the plumber, and I’ll completely miss what he said because I’m staring out the window at a squirrel. It’s embarrassing. He’s been so patient, but I can tell it’s wearing on him too. I just feel like I'm dropping the ball everywhere, all the time.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're supposed to be sitting still or focusing on a task?

Well, yes and no. I mean, I'm not running around the shop like a kid on a sugar rush or anything, but... it's more like this internal thing. Like, if I have to sit at the desk doing estimates—which I have to do a lot of, unfortunately, since I broke my wrist a few years back and had to take on more of the office work. Even though the wrist is healed now, I still get stuck with the paperwork. And when I'm sitting there, looking at all those numbers, or if I have to sit through a long meeting with a client or the crew... I just feel this awful, tight feeling inside. 

It's like I'm wound up like a cheap watch, you know? Like there's a motor humming in my chest and it just wants me to get up and move around. I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish the estimates. I tell myself, "Sarah, just sit here for twenty minutes and get this done." But my legs start bouncing, or I'm tapping my pen, or shifting in my chair constantly. It's almost physically uncomfortable to just be still. I'll find any excuse to get up—going to get coffee, checking the mail, asking someone a question that definitely could have waited. It’s like my body is rebelling against sitting still, even when my brain knows that's exactly what I need to be doing to get the job done.
Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you're unable to focus on a task?

Anxious? Hmm. You know, it's funny you ask it that way, because my husband, he'll ask me something similar. He'll say, "Sarah, are you stressed out about this?" But... no. Honestly, I wouldn't use the words anxious or overwhelmed. I think "overwhelmed" implies that I'm sitting there pulling my hair out in the moment, agonizing because my brain won't latch onto the work. But it’s actually kind of the exact opposite of that. 

When I lose my focus, I don't even realize it's happening, so there's no panic at all. I just... drift. It's like a boat slipping its moorings, you know? One minute I’m sanding down a nice piece of maple—and maple is tricky, you really have to pay attention to the grain or you’ll completely ruin the finish, especially if you’re moving up to a really fine grit paper—and the next minute, I’m completely engrossed in watching a dust mote float through a sunbeam coming in through the bay door. Or I’m suddenly trying to remember the name of that actor from that movie we watched back in, what, 1995? 

I'm not anxious in those moments at all. I'm actually perfectly content in whatever new, random direction my brain just dragged me. Like just this past Tuesday, I was supposed to be doing the payroll. And I don't feel overwhelmed by the math or anything, I've done the shop's payroll a million times. But I lost focus because I saw a tool catalog sitting on the very edge of the desk. It was one of those Rockler catalogs, they sell all these specialty jigs and clamps and things. And I spent forty-five minutes just looking at bar clamps. I wasn't anxious! I was having a perfectly nice time looking at clamps. 

It's only later, you know? It's only when the clock strikes five, or when one of the guys asks me for their check, and I look down and see the ledger just sitting there completely blank. That's when I get mad at myself. I get incredibly frustrated after the fact. But right when I'm actually failing to focus? No, no racing heart, no feeling of being overwhelmed. Just... poof. The focus is gone, and I'm off in my own little world without a care until reality taps me on the shoulder again.
Did your difficulties with focus and distraction start after something significant happened in your life, such as an accident, a move, or a change in your personal or work life?

Well, yes, actually. I brought it up just a minute ago, but it really all traces back to when I broke my wrist. That was... gosh, let me think, it was about a year and a month ago now. Just over a year. And it was my right wrist, too, which is just my luck since I’m right-handed. I was helping unload a delivery of heavy oak boards, and one of the younger guys lost his grip, the stack shifted, and I put my hand out to catch it—which is a stupid reflex, you know, you can't stop a hundred pounds of hardwood like that—and snap. Took me right out of commission for the physical stuff. 

So, because of that, I got shifted into doing all the shop paperwork and supervising the crew instead of doing the actual hands-on carpentry. And that... that right there is exactly when this level of trouble really started. I mean, before that, when I was working with my hands all day, measuring, cutting, routing... you’re moving, you're physically in the work, you know? It demands your attention in a different way. But being stuck behind a desk for the last thirteen months, having to supervise from afar and looking at spreadsheets and invoices instead of wood grain? It’s been a total disaster for my focus. If I hadn't had that accident and gotten moved into the office, I don't think things would be nearly this bad, but ever since that shift a year and a month ago, it's just been a constant, daily struggle to keep my head in the game.
Do you often interrupt others when they're speaking or finish their sentences for them?

Interrupting? Gosh, no, I don't think so. I really try to be mindful of that, actually. You see, growing up, my mother was a terrible interrupter. Just awful. You couldn't get a word in edgewise with her. She'd ask you a question about school or something, and before you could even get three words out, she was already talking over you about what she bought at the grocery store or what the neighbor was doing. It used to drive me absolutely crazy. So, because of that, I've always made a really conscious effort to let people finish what they're saying. 

Especially with the guys in the shop, you know? When you're managing a crew, communication is so important. If someone is trying to explain why a joint isn't fitting right or why they need a different type of fastener, you really have to listen to the whole explanation, because the devil is always in the details with carpentry. If you cut them off, you might miss the one crucial piece of information that explains the whole problem. And I certainly don't finish people's sentences for them. Honestly, half the time, I'm so distracted by whatever else is going on—like someone dropping a hammer on the other side of the shop or the sound of the air compressor kicking on—that I'm just trying my hardest to focus on the words they're actually saying to me right in that moment. So, no, interrupting really isn't something I struggle with. I might drift off while they're talking, sure, but I definitely let them finish talking before I respond.
Do you have trouble organizing your tasks or managing your time effectively?

Oh, my goodness, yes. It's an absolute nightmare. Like I was saying a minute ago about getting stuck doing all the shop paperwork... it's just been a complete disaster for my organization. 

You see, I don't even really use a proper office desk, I have this old drafting bench in the corner of the shop office. It's a beautiful old piece, solid oak, probably from the 1920s or 30s. I restored it myself a few years back. But right now? You can't even see the wood grain on top of it because of the sheer amount of paper just sitting there. Since I got moved to the office side of things, I sit down at that bench, I look at the mess, and I just... I cannot for the life of me figure out what needs doing first. It's like my brain just flatlines when I try to prioritize. 

I'll have a stack of bids that need to go out for new jobs—and bidding is so complicated right now with lumber prices fluctuating the way they do, you really have to stay on top of the suppliers' quotes—and right next to that, I've got the crew's schedules for the month, and then a pile of unpaid invoices from the hardware store, and then on top of all that, one of the apprentices will come wandering in and ask me a question about a cut list or a dovetail joint they're struggling with. And instead of handling one thing at a time, I just sort of... shuffle it all around. The bids, the schedules, the invoices, the apprentice questions, they all just pile up on my bench. I'll move a stack from the left side to the right side, think about doing the invoices, get distracted by the schedule, and get absolutely nowhere. 

And because I can't organize any of it in a sensible way, my time management just goes right out the window. I'll think I have all week to handle a bid, and suddenly it's Thursday afternoon and the papers are still just sitting there. Then I'm rushing like a madwoman, trying to get it all done in a blind panic, staying late, making myself crazy. And the worst part is, even with all that rushing at the eleventh hour, I’m still missing deadlines. I missed a deadline for a big custom kitchen cabinet bid just last week because the paperwork was buried under a stack of old receipts. I never used to be like this when I was actually building things. In carpentry, you follow a sequence, you know? You measure, you cut, you sand, you assemble. It makes sense. But this office work? I just can't find the sequence, and it all just piles up until I'm drowning in it.
Do you often feel the need to be active and have trouble engaging in quiet leisure activities?

Oh, absolutely. I just... I don't really do "quiet." Let me tell you about Sundays, for example. Sunday is supposed to be the day of rest, right? You go to service, you come home, you relax. But for me, it's just... well, it's torture, honestly. 

Even at church, when things are supposed to be quiet and reverent during the sermon, I just cannot handle it. I catch myself tapping my foot, shifting my weight around in the pew—and the pews at our church are this old, hard pine, so they creak every single time you move an inch, which just makes it worse. I'll be leaning over, whispering to my husband about something I just remembered, or commenting on the choir, and he'll just gently pat my knee to try and get me to settle down. But I can't! Sitting still in the quiet like that... it feels almost unbearable. It's like my skin is crawling. 

And it's exactly the same at home. If we try to just sit in the living room and read, or watch a slow movie, I end up getting up for no real reason at all. I'll tell him I'm going to get a glass of water, or check the thermostat, or see if the dog needs to go out—even if she literally just came inside ten minutes ago. I just have to be moving. The silence just echoes, you know? When I was working on the floor, there was always the hum of the table saws, the radio playing, people yelling over the noise. But quiet leisure time? It's not leisurely for me at all. I'll start tapping my fingers on the armrest, and before I know it, I'm up pacing around the kitchen looking for a hinge to oil or something to fiddle with, because just sitting there in the quiet is the hardest thing in the world for me.
Do you think your difficulty with focus and distraction is more related to not being able to pay attention or to being overly active and restless?

Well, gosh, that's a good question. I think... I mean, the distraction is bad, but the restlessness is just so overwhelming. It's a very physical thing for me. 

You see, I never used to do this much desk work in the first place. I actually had a bad fall a while back—slipped on some loose sawdust over by the large planer and went down hard on my hand. I really messed up my wrist. It was a whole ordeal, took months of physical therapy to get my grip strength back. So the boss moved me into the office to handle the bids and the paperwork while I recovered, just to keep me on the payroll. 

And the thing is, my wrist is completely healed now. The therapist cleared me, I can hold a hammer, I can run a saw, everything is perfectly fine. But they kept me doing all this administrative stuff anyway. And when I have to sit at that drafting bench doing those estimates, or if I have to sit through one of those really long, drawn-out production meetings with the general contractors where they just drone on and on about supply chain issues... I just feel so incredibly wound up inside. 

It's like there's a motor humming right in my chest, or a coiled spring, and I feel like I absolutely need to get up and move around. I sit there and I tell myself, you know, "Look, your wrist is healed, this is part of your job now, you know you're supposed to just stay put and finish this." I know I need to just sit there and get the estimate done. But the longer I sit there trying to force my brain to look at the numbers, the more that wound-up feeling builds and builds. It gets to the point where I'm practically jumping out of my skin, and I end up making up an excuse to go check on the crew just so I can walk around. So I really think it's that restless feeling that completely derails me, because I'm spending all my mental energy just trying to force my body to stay in that chair.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking through the consequences?

Act on impulse? Hmm. No, I really don't think I do that. Actually, it's funny you ask that, because my husband always says I'm the most overly cautious person he knows when it comes to actually making a move on something. 

You see, when you've been a carpenter as long as I have—gosh, it's been almost thirty-five years now—you just can't afford to be impulsive. It's drilled into you from day one as a green apprentice: measure twice, cut once. If you just go acting on impulse when you're standing in front of a cabinet saw spinning at four thousand RPMs, well, that's how people lose fingers. Or worse. And I still have all ten of mine, thank the Lord! I always tell the new kids in the shop, you have to respect the tools and you have to respect the wood, because neither of them will forgive you if you rush.

I mean, take the materials we work with. If I'm building a custom dining table out of, say, quarter-sawn white oak—which is just a beautiful wood, by the way, the medullary rays in it are absolutely gorgeous when you finish it right, but it is certainly not cheap. You can't just start hacking away at a piece of hardwood that costs that much a board foot without a solid, step-by-step plan. You have to map out every single cut, you have to account for the grain direction, the kerf of the blade... so my brain is very, very trained to think through the consequences of an action before I take it. 

Even now, with all this awful office work they have me doing... I might be bouncing my leg under that old drafting bench, and I might be completely incapable of deciding which invoice to look at first, but I'm not just... blindly signing checks or blurting things out to the suppliers or making rash decisions. If anything, with the paperwork, I'm the complete opposite of impulsive. I just stare at it, terrified of doing it wrong or messing up the math on a big bid, until I do absolutely nothing at all. So, no, I don't just jump into things without thinking them through. The restlessness is there, sure, like I said, but doing things on impulse? No, I really haven't noticed anything like that.
Do you think your mind wandering and difficulty with focus are more because you're not interested in the tasks or because you're constantly thinking about other things?

Well, it’s... it’s really the other things. Honestly, what brings me in here to see you in the first place is that I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. Not for the life of me. I mean, sure, the paperwork isn't exactly thrilling, but even when I sit down and tell myself I am going to finish a task, I just can't filter the rest of the world out. 

Like, I’ll be sitting there at that drafting table, trying to add up the board feet for a materials order, and out on the floor, one saw starts up. Just one! And because I've been doing this so long, I know the sound of every single machine in that shop. I hear the whine of the miter saw spinning up, and instantly, my brain is out there on the floor. I'm not looking at the numbers on my paper anymore; I'm wondering what they're cutting, who's running the saw, if they remembered to turn on the dust collector. Or somebody will just be walking past the office window—maybe one of the apprentices carrying a stack of plywood or sweeping up—and my eyes just automatically follow them. I lose my place on the page because I just have to see what they're doing. 

And the frustrating part is, it's not even just the stuff happening around me. It’s my own brain doing it to me, too. I could be staring at a completely quiet desk, and suddenly a thought about another job will just pop into my head out of absolutely nowhere. I'll be in the middle of a sentence, and I'll suddenly remember a custom bookshelf we installed last Tuesday, and I'll start wondering if the client ever decided on the stain color for the trim, or if we need to order more brackets for the next phase. 

And that one thought will completely pull me off what I’m doing. I'll start digging through old file cabinets to check the stain color on that other job, completely forgetting the materials order I was supposed to be finishing right then and there. Every little noise, every movement, every random thought... it all just yanks my attention away. And then I look up at the clock, and it's three in the afternoon, and I haven't finished a single estimate. The whole day just gets away from me. It happens every single day now, and it's just so incredibly frustrating.
Do you think your difficulty with sitting still and focusing is more because you have too much energy or because you just can't pay attention to the task at hand?

Well, gosh, it’s... it’s hard to completely separate the two, but honestly, I think it really comes down to having this... this physical energy, or whatever you want to call it, that just won't let me be. Because it’s not just happening when I’m trying to focus on a specific task at the shop. It happens even when there is absolutely no task at all, when I’m just supposed to be resting or being quiet. 

Even at home in the evenings, or, oh my goodness, especially in church... when things are supposed to be perfectly quiet and peaceful, I just cannot handle it. We go to Sunday service, and the whole congregation will be sitting there, dead silent, listening to the sermon, and I catch myself tapping my foot against the pew, or constantly shifting my weight around from one side to the other. I'll lean over and start whispering to my husband about something completely unrelated, or I'll just get up and walk to the back of the sanctuary or go to the restroom for absolutely no real reason at all. 

And my husband, bless his heart, he notices it constantly. We’ll be sitting in the living room on a Friday night, supposedly just relaxing and watching a movie, and I'm still doing it. I'm tapping my fingers on the armrest, I'm getting up to adjust the throw pillows, I'm pacing into the kitchen for a glass of water I don't even want. It's just that sitting still in the quiet feels almost unbearable to me. It really does. It’s like the quieter the room gets, the louder that restless, wound-up feeling gets inside my body, and I just have to do something, anything, to let it out. So, yes, I think it’s really that physical energy driving it, because even when I don't need to pay attention to anything at all, I still can't just sit there in the quiet.
Did you experience difficulties with focus, distraction, or restlessness when you were a child, before the age of 12?

Oh, my goodness, yes. It goes way, way back. You know, it’s funny you bring up being a kid, because my mother, rest her soul, she used to absolutely pull her hair out over me when I was little. I mean, way back in grade school, long before I even turned twelve or went off to junior high. 

I can still picture it. Every single parent-teacher conference, it was the exact same story, year after year. Mrs. Gable in third grade, Mr. Henderson in fifth... they would all sit my mother down in those tiny little classroom chairs and tell her, "She’s such a bright girl, she really is, but she is just so careless." That was the word they always used. Careless. And it broke my heart, because it wasn't that I didn't want to do the work or that I was trying to be difficult. Things would just... disappear on me. I'd do my spelling homework at the kitchen table, I swear I would, and then the next morning it would just vanish somewhere between my front door and my desk at school. I was constantly losing my homework. 

And the instructions! The teacher would stand at the chalkboard and give us a list of things to do—like, "take out your math workbook, turn to page forty-two, and do the odd numbers"—and by the time I managed to fish my pencil and my book out of my desk, I'd completely forgotten what page we were supposed to be on or what we were even doing. 

But the worst part, the thing that really got me in trouble, was the windows. If they put my desk anywhere near a window, well, you could just forget about me getting anything done. I was supposed to be finishing my seatwork, practicing my cursive or doing long division, and instead, I'd just be staring out the glass. I remember one year they were building a new cafeteria across the schoolyard, and I would just watch those guys framing the walls and pouring the concrete for hours. I was absolutely mesmerized by it, just staring out the window while my worksheet sat there completely blank on my desk. My mother tried everything to get me to pay attention, she really did, but it was just always like that. So, yes, the losing things, the drifting off... it’s been happening since I was a little girl.
Do you experience these difficulties with focus and restlessness at home or in other situations outside of work?

Oh, it’s everywhere. It really is. It spills over into absolutely every single part of my life, not just at the shop, though Lord knows it’s bad enough there. I mean, I know I was just talking about getting distracted at work, but it’s not just a minor annoyance anymore—it’s actually causing real damage to the business. My mistakes and my delays, they’ve actually cost me commissions lately. I'll get so sidetracked that I miss a deadline for a bid, or I'll mess up a measurement on the paperwork. Just recently, we had to do a complete rework on a job because I lost my focus and ordered the wrong dimensions for the materials. And the crew... well, you work with these guys for years, they’re like family, but even they are getting fed up with me. I can tell they are just a lot less willing to rely on me for the scheduling or the ordering anymore. They'll kind of quietly go around me to double-check the delivery dates, and it just hurts my pride so much. But I can't even blame them, because I keep dropping the ball!

And then I go home, hoping I can just pull it together, but it’s the exact same story there. My poor husband—I mentioned him earlier, bless his heart—he has had to completely take over all the household bills and the daily reminders. He just had to step in and do it. Because I would bring the mail in, set it down on the kitchen island to go do something else, and then completely forget it existed. I just keep misplacing important papers left and right, or I'll just completely miss what needs to be done around the house. A bill would sit under a pile of grocery circulars until we got a final notice. It's just embarrassing, honestly. At my age, you’d think I could manage to pay a simple bill on time, but I just lose track of the papers and the deadlines. So now he just handles all of it, and I feel terrible putting all that extra weight on his shoulders, but if he didn't do it, nothing would get paid. It just feels like I'm letting everybody down, everywhere I go.
Are your difficulties with focus, distraction, and restlessness causing problems in your relationships or daily life outside of work?

Well, gosh, like I... I know I was just rambling on about this a second ago, but yes, absolutely. It is causing a tremendous amount of trouble, and it just breaks my heart to admit it. 

I mean, I mentioned the commissions and having to redo that job, but you have to understand, in carpentry, materials are not cheap! Lumber prices being what they are, when I lose my focus and order the wrong dimensions, and we have to do a complete rework... well, that comes right out of the bottom line. It’s cost me actual commissions. And the guys on the crew, they are such good men, but I can see it in their eyes. They don't want to rely on me for the scheduling anymore. They don't trust me to order the right supplies. They’ll just quietly go around me to handle the delivery dates themselves, and it just stings, you know? It really stings, because I'm the one who's supposed to be on top of it, and I'm just making these careless mistakes and delaying everything.

And then at home... well, like I said about my poor husband taking over the bills, it’s not just the financial stuff, it’s all the daily reminders, too. He has had to completely take the reins. Because I will walk into the house with important papers—notices, receipts, whatever it is—and I’ll just set them down somewhere and they might as well have ceased to exist. I keep misplacing everything. I'll completely miss what needs to be done around the house, like a chore I promised I'd do, unless he explicitly reminds me. He’s basically managing my whole life for me at this point because I just can't keep track of the papers or the responsibilities. It makes me feel awful, like I'm not pulling my weight as a partner, but if he didn't step in and do it, everything would just fall apart.
Did you have difficulty with focus, distraction, or restlessness as a child?

Well, gosh, I know I was just talking your ear off about this a little bit ago, but yes, absolutely. It goes way, way back, definitely before I was twelve. Even back in grade school, it was just a constant, everyday struggle. My poor mother, she had to sit through so many of those awful parent-teacher conferences, and it was always the exact same story from every single teacher. They were always telling my mother that I was a bright girl, which was nice of them to say, I suppose, but then they would always follow it up by saying I was just so careless. 

And hearing that just breaks a kid's heart, because I really wasn't trying to be bad or cause trouble! But I was constantly losing my homework. I mean, I would do it, I swear I would, and then it would just completely vanish before I could turn it in. And forgetting instructions... oh, my goodness. The teacher would tell us what to do, and the instructions would just evaporate from my brain the second she stopped talking. So instead of finishing my seatwork like all the other kids were doing, I would just be sitting there at my desk, completely zoned out, staring out the window for heaven knows how long. Just watching whatever was happening outside instead of finishing my seatwork. So, yes, doctor, it really has been this way for pretty much my entire life.
Are your difficulties with focus, distraction, and restlessness significantly impacting your overall well-being or relationships?

Well, yes, doctor, it really, really is. I mean, I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record at this point, just repeating myself, but it really is taking such a heavy toll on everything. It’s just so overwhelming. 

Like I was saying about work... it’s not just a little oops here and there anymore. It’s my livelihood, you know? I’ve been a carpenter for a long time, and I take pride in my work, but lately... well, my mistakes and the delays, they’ve literally cost me commissions. Real money out of my pocket. And that job where we had to do the complete rework because I messed up the materials order? That was just devastating. It’s humiliating, honestly. And the crew... they’re good guys, they really are, but I can see it. They just aren't willing to rely on me for the scheduling or the ordering anymore. They’re stepping around me to get things done, and it just makes me feel so inadequate, like I'm failing at the one thing I'm supposed to be good at.

And then, of course, it spills right over into my home life, which is just as bad, if not worse, because that’s my family. My husband, bless him, he’s a saint for putting up with me, but he’s had to completely take over all the bills and all the daily reminders. Every single one of them. Because if it were up to me, I’d just keep misplacing the papers or completely missing what needs to be done. I just can't hold onto a thought long enough to follow through with it. It makes me feel like such a burden on him, like I'm not a real partner in this marriage anymore. So, yes, it’s definitely impacting my well-being and my relationships in a very big, very painful way. It just feels like my brain is working against me every step of the way, and everyone around me is having to pay the price for it.
Did your parents or teachers ever mention that you had significant difficulties with focus or restlessness when you were very young?

Well, gosh, I... I know I just mentioned this a minute ago, and I'm probably talking your ear off again, but yes, it really was exactly like that. It goes way, way back. Definitely before I was twelve years old, back in grade school. 

I can still picture my poor mother coming home from those parent-teacher conferences. She'd sit me down at the kitchen table, and it was always the exact same story, year after year, teacher after teacher. They would always start by telling her that I was a bright girl—which, you know, is a nice thing to hear, I suppose, trying to soften the blow—but then they would immediately follow it up by saying how terribly careless I was. 

And it just... it breaks your heart when you're a kid, because I wasn't trying to be difficult! But I was constantly losing my homework. I'd sit at that table, I'd do the work, and then by the time I got to school, it had just completely vanished. And the instructions... oh, the teacher would stand up there and explain what we were supposed to do, and the second she stopped talking, it was like the words just evaporated right out of my brain. So instead of finishing my seatwork like all the other kids in the row, I'd just be sitting there, completely zoned out, staring out the window at the playground or the trees or heaven knows what. Just completely lost in my own world instead of doing what I was supposed to be doing. So, yes, they definitely noticed it very early on.
Have you been experiencing these difficulties with focus, distraction, and restlessness for more than 6 months?

Oh, yes, definitely more than six months. I mean, like I was saying before, I’ve always had my struggles going all the way back to when I was a little girl in school, but *this* level of trouble? Where it’s just completely ruining my work and making me feel like I’m losing my mind on a daily basis? That has been going on for right about a year and a month now. 

I know the exact timeline because, well, it all really escalated when I broke my wrist. Just a silly, stupid accident, really. I slipped and put my hand out to catch myself, and you know how it goes. At my age, it took a good long while to heal up properly. But because of the cast and then all the physical therapy I had to do, I couldn't do the actual hands-on carpentry anymore. Which just broke my heart, honestly, because I’ve always loved the physical work. There's just something about the feel of the wood and being right in the middle of building something tangible. 

But, bless them, they wanted to keep me on, so they shifted me over into doing the shop paperwork and handling the supervising instead. And oh, my goodness, doctor, that is exactly when the bottom just completely fell out. Going from working with my hands and moving around all day to suddenly having to sit still at a desk, staring at invoices and materials lists, and trying to organize schedules for the rest of the crew... it's been about thirteen months of just absolute torture. My brain just cannot handle sitting there trying to focus on all those little details on paper, and the restlessness of being stuck in a chair just makes it impossible to concentrate. So, yes, to answer your question, it’s been a little over a year—a year and a month, exactly—since things got this severe with the paperwork and all the supervising.

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, honestly, what brings me in is... I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. And I mean, I've been doing carpentry since I got out of high school, almost forty years, so I know my way around a shop. I know how to work. But lately, it's like every little thing pulls me away. 

I'll be in the middle of measuring a cut, and just one saw starting up across the floor—just that noise—and I'm completely derailed. I'm wondering who's running it, if they're using the right blade, what they're working on. Or somebody walking past the office window. I'll stop what I'm doing just to see who it is and where they're going. 

Sometimes it's not even something happening around me, it's just my own head. Like, I’ll get a random thought about another job we've got lined up for next week, and suddenly I'm walking away from my workbench to go check the lumber order for that other job, completely abandoning the piece that's right in front of me. I’ll look at the clock and it’s quitting time, and I haven’t finished the one simple cabinet door I started at eight in the morning. It’s just... it’s exhausting, to be honest with you, because I'm trying so hard to just do the work, but I just get pulled off what I’m doing constantly, every single day, and I can't afford to keep losing time like this.

Well, yes and no. I mean, I'm not running around the shop like a kid on a sugar rush or anything, but... it's more like this internal thing. Like, if I have to sit at the desk doing estimates—which I have to do a lot of, unfortunately, since I broke my wrist a few years back and had to take on more of the office work. Even though the wrist is healed now, I still get stuck with the paperwork. And when I'm sitting there, looking at all those numbers, or if I have to sit through a long meeting with a client or the crew... I just feel this awful, tight feeling inside.

I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish the estimates. I tell myself, "Sarah, just sit here for twenty minutes and get this done." doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are associated with emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you're unable to focus on a task?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of anxiety or being overwhelmed when unable to focus, which is not covered by any of the specific ADHD symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
Anxious? Hmm. You know, it's funny you ask it that way, because my husband, he'll ask me something similar. He'll say, "Sarah, are you stressed out about this?" But... no. Honestly, I wouldn't use the words anxious or overwhelmed. I think "overwhelmed" implies that I'm sitting there pulling my hair out in the moment, agonizing because my brain won't latch onto the work. But it’s actually kind of the exact opposite of that. 

When I lose my focus, I don't even realize it's happening, so there's no panic at all. I just... drift. It's like a boat slipping its moorings, you know? One minute I’m sanding down a nice piece of maple—and maple is tricky, you really have to pay attention to the grain or you’ll completely ruin the finish, especially if you’re moving up to a really fine grit paper—and the next minute, I’m completely engrossed in watching a dust mote float through a sunbeam coming in through the bay door. Or I’m suddenly trying to remember the name of that actor from that movie we watched back in, what, 1995? 

I'm not anxious in those moments at all. I'm actually perfectly content in whatever new, random direction my brain just dragged me. Like just this past Tuesday, I was supposed to be doing the payroll. And I don't feel overwhelmed by the math or anything, I've done the shop's payroll a million times. But I lost focus because I saw a tool catalog sitting on the very edge of the desk. It was one of those Rockler catalogs, they sell all these specialty jigs and clamps and things. And I spent forty-five minutes just looking at bar clamps. I wasn't anxious! I was having a perfectly nice time looking at clamps. 

It's only later, you know? It's only when the clock strikes five, or when one of the guys asks me for their check, and I look down and see the ledger just sitting there completely blank. That's when I get mad at myself. I get incredibly frustrated after the fact. But right when I'm actually failing to focus? No, no racing heart, no feeling of being overwhelmed. Just... poof. The focus is gone, and I'm off in my own little world without a care until reality taps me on the shoulder again.

Interrupting? Gosh, no, I don't think so. I really try to be mindful of that, actually. You see, growing up, my mother was a terrible interrupter. Just awful. You couldn't get a word in edgewise with her. She'd ask you a question about school or something, and before you could even get three words out, she was already talking over you about what she bought at the grocery store or what the neighbor was doing. It used to drive me absolutely crazy. So, because of that, I've always made a really conscious effort to let people finish what they're saying. 

Especially with the guys in the shop, you know? When you're managing a crew, communication is so important. If someone is trying to explain why a joint isn't fitting right or why they need a different type of fastener, you really have to listen to the whole explanation, because the devil is always in the details with carpentry. If you cut them off, you might miss the one crucial piece of information that explains the whole problem. And I certainly don't finish people's sentences for them. Honestly, half the time, I'm so distracted by whatever else is going on—like someone dropping a hammer on the other side of the shop or the sound of the air compressor kicking on—that I'm just trying my hardest to focus on the words they're actually saying to me right in that moment. So, no, interrupting really isn't something I struggle with. I might drift off while they're talking, sure, but I definitely let them finish talking before I respond.

Oh, absolutely. I just... I don't really do "quiet." Let me tell you about Sundays, for example. Sunday is supposed to be the day of rest, right? You go to service, you come home, you relax. But for me, it's just... well, it's torture, honestly. 

Even at church, when things are supposed to be quiet and reverent during the sermon, I just cannot handle it. I catch myself tapping my foot, shifting my weight around in the pew—and the pews at our church are this old, hard pine, so they creak every single time you move an inch, which just makes it worse. I'll be leaning over, whispering to my husband about something I just remembered, or commenting on the choir, and he'll just gently pat my knee to try and get me to settle down. But I can't! Sitting still in the quiet like that... it feels almost unbearable. It's like my skin is crawling. 

And it's exactly the same at home. If we try to just sit in the living room and read, or watch a slow movie, I end up getting up for no real reason at all. I'll tell him I'm going to get a glass of water, or check the thermostat, or see if the dog needs to go out—even if she literally just came inside ten minutes ago. I just have to be moving. The silence just echoes, you know? When I was working on the floor, there was always the hum of the table saws, the radio playing, people yelling over the noise. But quiet leisure time? It's not leisurely for me at all. I'll start tapping my fingers on the armrest, and before I know it, I'm up pacing around the kitchen looking for a hinge to oil or something to fiddle with, because just sitting there in the quiet is the hardest thing in the world for me.

Well, gosh, that's a good question. I think... I mean, the distraction is bad, but the restlessness is just so overwhelming. It's a very physical thing for me. 

You see, I never used to do this much desk work in the first place. I actually had a bad fall a while back—slipped on some loose sawdust over by the large planer and went down hard on my hand. I really messed up my wrist. It was a whole ordeal, took months of physical therapy to get my grip strength back. So the boss moved me into the office to handle the bids and the paperwork while I recovered, just to keep me on the payroll. 

And the thing is, my wrist is completely healed now. The therapist cleared me, I can hold a hammer, I can run a saw, everything is perfectly fine. But they kept me doing all this administrative stuff anyway. And when I have to sit at that drafting bench doing those estimates, or if I have to sit through one of those really long, drawn-out production meetings with the general contractors where they just drone on and on about supply chain issues... I just feel so incredibly wound up inside. 

It's like there's a motor humming right in my chest, or a coiled spring, and I feel like I absolutely need to get up and move around. I sit there and I tell myself, you know, "Look, your wrist is healed, this is part of your job now, you know you're supposed to just stay put and finish this." I know I need to just sit there and get the estimate done. But the longer I sit there trying to force my brain to look at the numbers, the more that wound-up feeling builds and builds. It gets to the point where I'm practically jumping out of my skin, and I end up making up an excuse to go check on the crew just so I can walk around. So I really think it's that restless feeling that completely derails me, because I'm spending all my mental energy just trying to force my body to stay in that chair.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily driven by impulsivity
doctor.question: Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking through the consequences?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about impulsivity, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Act on impulse? Hmm. No, I really don't think I do that. Actually, it's funny you ask that, because my husband always says I'm the most overly cautious person he knows when it comes to actually making a move on something. 

You see, when you've been a carpenter as long as I have—gosh, it's been almost thirty-five years now—you just can't afford to be impulsive. It's drilled into you from day one as a green apprentice: measure twice, cut once. If you just go acting on impulse when you're standing in front of a cabinet saw spinning at four thousand RPMs, well, that's how people lose fingers. Or worse. And I still have all ten of mine, thank the Lord! I always tell the new kids in the shop, you have to respect the tools and you have to respect the wood, because neither of them will forgive you if you rush.

I mean, take the materials we work with. If I'm building a custom dining table out of, say, quarter-sawn white oak—which is just a beautiful wood, by the way, the medullary rays in it are absolutely gorgeous when you finish it right, but it is certainly not cheap. You can't just start hacking away at a piece of hardwood that costs that much a board foot without a solid, step-by-step plan. You have to map out every single cut, you have to account for the grain direction, the kerf of the blade... so my brain is very, very trained to think through the consequences of an action before I take it. 

Even now, with all this awful office work they have me doing... I might be bouncing my leg under that old drafting bench, and I might be completely incapable of deciding which invoice to look at first, but I'm not just... blindly signing checks or blurting things out to the suppliers or making rash decisions. If anything, with the paperwork, I'm the complete opposite of impulsive. I just stare at it, terrified of doing it wrong or messing up the math on a big bid, until I do absolutely nothing at all. So, no, I don't just jump into things without thinking them through. The restlessness is there, sure, like I said, but doing things on impulse? No, I really haven't noticed anything like that.

Well, it’s... it’s really the other things. Honestly, what brings me in here to see you in the first place is that I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. Not for the life of me. I mean, sure, the paperwork isn't exactly thrilling, but even when I sit down and tell myself I am going to finish a task, I just can't filter the rest of the world out. 

Like, I’ll be sitting there at that drafting table, trying to add up the board feet for a materials order, and out on the floor, one saw starts up. Just one! And because I've been doing this so long, I know the sound of every single machine in that shop. I hear the whine of the miter saw spinning up, and instantly, my brain is out there on the floor.
